Compare two networks descriptively

Source: R/compare_network.R
compare_model.Rd

compare_model() compares two networks, or two weight matrices, edge by edge and returns a battery of descriptive agreement measures: weight deviations (mean, median, root-mean-square and maximum absolute difference, relative mean absolute difference, coefficient-of-variation ratio), four correlations (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, distance correlation), five dissimilarities (Euclidean, Manhattan, Canberra, Bray-Curtis, Frobenius), five similarities (cosine, Jaccard, Dice, overlap, RV coefficient) and two pattern agreements (rank and sign agreement), with the two networks' metrics side by side and, on request, their centrality differences. It takes two netobjects, cograph_networks or square numeric matrices, or two members of a netobject_group. Both weight matrices are scaled with the same scaling before comparison, which decides how weights from different estimators are put on a common footing.

The measures describe how alike the two estimated networks are; they say nothing about whether a difference is larger than sampling variation would produce. For that, test the difference with permutation() (two transition networks) or with nct() on the two groups' observations (psychological networks). compare_networks() compares any number of networks with tidy tables and a plot() that draws one view per call.

Usage

compare_model(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netobject'
compare_model(
  x,
  y,
  scaling = "none",
  measures = character(0),
  network = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'cograph_network'
compare_model(
  x,
  y,
  scaling = "none",
  measures = character(0),
  network = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'matrix'
compare_model(
  x,
  y,
  scaling = "none",
  measures = character(0),
  network = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'netobject_group'
compare_model(
  x,
  i = 1L,
  j = 2L,
  scaling = "none",
  measures = character(0),
  network = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'net_comparison'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_comparison'
plot(
  x,
  type = c("scatter", "heatmap", "diff_hist", "weight_dist", "all"),
  combined = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

The first network: a netobject, a cograph_network or a numeric square matrix, or a netobject_group whose members i and j are compared. For the print() and plot() methods: a net_comparison object.

...

Not used.

y

The second network, in the same forms (not used for a netobject_group). The two must hold the same nodes and have no missing weights. Named inputs are aligned by node name, so the node order may differ; different node sets, or missing, empty or duplicated names, raise an error. A matrix without names is matched to the other input by position and takes its node names; when neither input has names the nodes are labelled V1, V2, ....

scaling

The scaling applied to each weight matrix before comparison. Default "none". One of:

"none"

The weights as they are.

"minmax"

\((w - \min) / (\max - \min)\), which maps them to \([0, 1]\); a constant matrix is left as it is.

"max"

\(w / \max|w|\), dividing by the largest absolute weight, so signs are kept; a matrix of zeros is left as it is.

"rank"

Average ranks, mapped to \([0, 1]\) by min-max; an ordinal scaling. A constant matrix keeps its (equal) ranks.

"zscore"

\((w - \bar w) / s_w\), the standard score; a constant matrix is only centred.

"robust"

\((w - \mathrm{med}(w)) / \mathrm{mad}(w)\), a standard score from the median and the median absolute deviation, less affected by outliers; with a MAD of 0 the weights are only centred.

"log"

\(\log(w)\); needs \(w > 0\): a weight at or below 0 raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input (use "log1p" for networks with zeros).

"log1p"

\(\log(1 + w)\); defined for \(w > -1\). A weight of -1 or below makes the comparison fail with an error.

"softmax"

A numerically stable softmax over all the cells.

"quantile"

The empirical cumulative distribution of the cells.

"frobenius"

The matrix divided by its Frobenius norm \(\|W\|_F = \sqrt{\sum w_{ij}^2}\), a matrix-level normalisation.

"row"

Each row divided by the sum of its absolute values, so the rows sum to 1 for non-negative weights; rows summing to zero are left unchanged.

Scalings that produce negative weights ("zscore", "robust") work with network = TRUE: the side-by-side distances are computed on the absolute weights.

measures

Centrality measures to compare. Default character(0) (none). Any built-in measure of net_centrality() can be named: "OutStrength", "InStrength", "ClosenessIn", "ClosenessOut", "Closeness", "Betweenness", "BetweennessRSP", "Diffusion" and "Clustering" ("InCloseness" and "OutCloseness" are accepted for "ClosenessIn" and "ClosenessOut"). Unknown names are dropped with a warning. The centralities are computed on the scaled matrices as directed networks, without self-loops.

network

Whether to add the two networks' metrics side by side (the metrics summary() reports for a netobject). Default TRUE.

i, j

For a netobject_group: the two members to compare, by index or name. Defaults 1 and 2; the two must differ, and a member that does not exist raises an error.

type

For plot(): the view. "scatter" (default) plots each cell's weight in y against its weight in x, with the line of perfect agreement (dashed), an OLS fit with its 95% band and the Pearson, Spearman and Kendall correlations. "heatmap" draws the difference matrix x - y on the diverging palette: blue where x is larger, red where y is larger, white where they agree. "diff_hist" is a histogram of the absolute differences |x - y|, with a density curve, a rug of the cells and lines at the mean and median. "weight_dist" overlays the distributions of |x| and |y|. "all" draws these four views in a 2 x 2 grid.

combined

For plot() with type = "all": TRUE (default) arranges the four views into one 2 x 2 gtable, which needs the gridExtra package; FALSE returns them as a named list of ggplots, to print, save or lay out separately. Ignored for the other views.

Value

A net_comparison object. Print it for the agreement measures, the side-by-side network metrics and the centrality correlations; plot() draws the edge-weight scatter or another view (see type). The object is a list with:

matrices

The two scaled weight matrices, x and y, aligned by node.

difference_matrix

The scaled x minus the scaled y.

edge_metrics

A data frame with one row per cell (source, target, self-loops included): the two weights and their raw, absolute, squared, relative and rank differences, percentile difference, ratio (similarity_strength_index), relative change (difference_index), log ratio of 1 + weight (logarithmic_ratio, NA where a weight is -1 or below), standardised weights and their ratio. A ratio is NA where its denominator is zero, and the standardised weights are NA when a matrix is constant.

summary_metrics

A data frame of the 22 agreement measures, with columns category, metric and value.

network_metrics

When network = TRUE: a data frame with columns metric, x and y, one row per network metric.

centrality_differences, centrality_correlations

When measures is not empty (empty data frames when none of its names is valid): one row per node and measure (state, centrality, x, y, difference), and one row per measure with the correlation of the two networks' values.

print() returns its input invisibly. plot() returns a ggplot; with type = "all", it draws the 2 x 2 grid and returns it invisibly as a gtable, or with combined = FALSE returns the four ggplots invisibly as a named list.

Details

The measures, scalings and edge metrics mirror tna::compare() (tna 1.5.4 and later) numerically. The distance correlation is that of Szekely, Rizzo and Bakirov (2007), NA when one network is constant, and the RV coefficient that of Robert and Escoufier (1976). A network's own directed flag decides how its network metrics are computed; a plain matrix has none, so an asymmetric matrix is read as directed and a symmetric one as undirected.

References

Szekely, G. J., Rizzo, M. L., & Bakirov, N. K. (2007). Measuring and testing dependence by correlation of distances. The Annals of Statistics, 35(6), 2769–2794. doi:10.1214/009053607000000505

Robert, P., & Escoufier, Y. (1976). A unifying tool for linear multivariate statistical methods: The RV-coefficient. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics), 25(3), 257–265. doi:10.2307/2347233

Examples

nets <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                      actor = "Actor", action = "Action", time = "Time",
                      group = "Achiever")
compare_model(nets)
